item.title: Re: Blood Bowl Hell (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you very much for your response; it's honestly really appreciated.

I understand your qualms. I personally believe that a story can portray cruelty in a socially responsible manner, as long as it unambiguously establishes that such cruelty is wrong, ala Silence of the Lambs. I also would have to make sure that these characters are not empty vessels existing only for suffering, but fleshed out characters who just so happen to also suffer. Just out of curiosity, in what place(s) do I cross the line in your eyes, so I can avoid doing so in the future?

Also, regarding the Shinto vs Buddhism thing: the reason I wanted it to be a Shinto priest was actually because they aren't Buddhist. I wanted it to come off as a "the Buddhists say this, but it's not my religion and it all seems kinda freaky to me" kinda thing. I completely understand though that it came off like I didn't know what I was talking about. Are there any other instances in there that seem to indicate a lack of understanding on my part?

Again, thank you very much for responding. While you clearly don't like my idea, I appreciate you taking the time out of your day to read it and explain your qualms. Merry Christmas!

item.title: (Looking for greenlight) The Ever-Hunger
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlight Yes
Page Type SCP Article
Genre Horror

Elevator Pitch
This anomaly does not have an appearance but from signs of consuming its designated slot and neighboring slots through usages of biting and tearing texts and images apart.

The document/data concerning this entity must be periodically moved to a different slot when signs of consumption and degradation start to show in the file.

If the entity does not get relocated, then it will start devouring neighboring SCPs, "deleting" them from the database" and literally, making them become non-existent along with related sites, staff, and personnel.

This SCP is not a virus in the database as it has the ability to erase things it consumes from existence in the SCP universe. The location where the deleted site/anomalies used to be will be replaced with a black void, signifying a hole in reality itself. Because of the reality bending effects it left, it is designated an infohazard/cognitohazard Keter anomaly. Observing the tear in reality caused the observers to become "aware" of its fictional status, and aware of entities from higher dimensions (the authors) who have the power to influence and shape their universe.

This ever-hunger entity can cause an end-of-reality scenario if left unchecked, so the O5 planned to cause global extinction as being terminated is a better fate than to be "deleted", or so they belived.

Central Narrative
This will be presented by normal means of containing (constant relocation of the anomaly) while hiding its true nature (that it cannot be permanently contained and that it caused things to become non-existent). And fake description/containment procedures to keep people from panicking and becoming aware of their fictional world. This implies that in the future, it may devours its designated slot faster than the foundation could even react.

Experimental logs involving D-Class getting send into the void, MTF getting erased from the database as they explore the deleted site and list of "known" deleted anomalies that the foundation somehow still have the record.

Hook/Attention-Grabber
The document ending will be left vague after all the interviews, logs, failed neutralization attempt and how the GOC tried to use this anomaly without knowing the after-effect. This will left the reader to imagine if they all died (from O5 explosion), wiped out from the conflict between GOC and the foundation, or something else entirely.

Additional Notes
None

item.title: The Humanoids
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights:** Yes.

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror/Comedy

Elevator Pitch: A mysterious software appears along with a mysterious PC out of nowhere and seems to grant mindless beings knowledge to act as sapient beings. However, they can't recall their past nor origin and seem to have only a small piece of their memories.

Central Narrative:

+ show block
– hide block

This software was discovered when one of the Foundation personnel noticed strange sounds from one of the enhanced containment chambers that're containing non-sapient SCPs. They discovered that it is talking and chatting on a PC that shows up out of nowhere.

This SCP originally is a PC that appears to have an unknown chatroom with unidentified programmers. This chatroom's software is named "The Humanoids," seemingly designed for both sapient and non-sapient anomalies to interact with each other through the technology screens. Any non-sapient/mindless humanoid entities/beings who come in contact with the screen will eventually be granted the knowledge to act as beings that aren't mindless. Of course, they may also embody human nature and act like regular humans, and some act very smart.

However, despite being granted sapient knowledge, the humanoid entities cannot remember their origins, and some seem only to recall a small piece of their memories.

Attempted to delete the software or destroy the PC is proven to be impossible, for it is shown to be constructed out of mysterious unidentified materials and seemingly has a powerful firewall to prevent hackers from infiltrating into it. However, the Foundation didn't try their best efforts in an attempt to erase the software nor wreck the PC, for it is because, with the help of "The Humanoids" chatroom, the hostile non-sapient SCPs appear to have good behaviors rather than being hostile, evil, and aggressive. However, the chatroom doesn't actually change the behaviors of sapient SCPs as they still have their original personalities.


Hook/Attention-Grabber: For those of you who have watched or read "Durarara" then this SCP was inspired by the "Dollar's" chatroom of the "Durarara" series.

Additional Notes: Draft is work in progress.

item.title: Forum Criticism Team - Captain Post
item.content:encoded:
Author, per the Draft Forum's new policy: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-10629348/new-draft-forum-policies authors who have not yet posted a successful mainsite article are now required to get their basic concept(s) greenlighted by two experienced reviewers in the Ideas Critique forum and/or IRC chatrooms before asking for draft feedback.

Please first go to the Ideas forum or the chat, give a quick summary (for the Ideas forum, please follow the instructions in the required reading thread) of the concept you want to write up (don't link the draft unless someone requests it), and reviewers can help you make sure that your core idea is something that will be successful with the community audience.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can also help by letting you know if something similar already exists on the site, and/or telling you if there are any cliches/pitfalls/other typical downvote reasons to be careful of with your particular idea. These issues are more effectively addressed earlier on in the writing process.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note from whom and where you received them. If you would like to receive draft critique without going through the greenlighting process, please use the IRC chatrooms to request reviews.

item.title: Re: Jejunu: The Curious Embodiment of a Manmade Famine (Looking for Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

What like…actually is 'Jejunu'? Is it a person? A creature? An object? Some weird hostile meme that doesn't exist as a physical thing but as the noosphere embodiment of the concept of 'famine'? How does Jejunu tie into the 'manmade famine' thing?

A few interviews and tests lead to the discovery of it’s abilities and it’s constant need to eat.

So like…what are it's abilities? How do the interviews and tests lead to this discovery? What makes this discovery interesting for a reader to read about?

Jejunu makes an escape, learns a few things about the facility, and is subsequently placed back into confinement with ease.

How did it manage to escape if it was so easily reconfined?

With each interview it becomes more uncomfortable and hungry until an incident inevitably happens.

What incident?

I guess to summarise my feelings on this, I would say that I don't really have a clear idea of what you're doing to offer much in depth feedback. My largest concern isn't so much 'I don't really have an idea of what this is' so much as that I am concerned that all of the narrative is focussed around info-dumping about the SCP, when really I want to see some kinda…exploration of why this thing existing is interesting.

It also feels like it's strongly lacking a hook: there's this kinda, progression of events that kinda works but there's not really a driving force moving from one to the next or a sense of the events building up to something or something, y'know?

item.title: Re: [Seeking Greenlights] Big Red Button
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

I think at the core of this, my issue with your pitch is that I don't find any of the individual elements interesting and I also don't find the way the elements come together particularly interesting.

The creation/destruction of whole timelines is something that's really hard to pull off in an article well because like…it's really hard to relate to big numbers changing? Like, this really needs a human face and like, someone who we can relate to that this affects: see e.g. SCP-5552 where like, yeah, the narrative involves massive death and huge changes and stakes; but like, it works because it's focussed in on a few researchers trying to make things work, and academic theft.

Following this: the central narrative section doesn't actually do anything interesting with the huge world ending stakes: there's this vague thing about the Foundation stopping it being used; and them needing the blue button as a last resort; but there's not really any indications of like….stuff happening to show why it's a bad idea to use this or how the blue button could be used as a last resort or anything.

You mention having 'an incident report, an interview log, testing logs, and addenda' but I have literally 0 idea of what you're actually doing with them.

item.title: Re: A narrative about the foundation censoring stuff again.
item.content:encoded:
[+] Open for crit
– hide block

Yeah, idk. I think really my question here is why the Foundation would write a SCP article about this: it's something they made and are utilising, and it's not even necessarily that anomalous; so it seems like all an in-universe article about this would do would be create a way by which people could realise this is the case when they shouldn't?

This kinda feels like it'd work best as a tale: I can totally see this really cool intrigue piece where like, someone working at a UIU/Foundation site realises that something weird is going on and like, gradually starts piecing stuff together before realising that hey, they aren't actually in the Foundation and are actually a member of the UIU and then they have to try and do something to put an end to this without being discovered and amnesticised.

My problem with this as a SCP is that effectively the article is positioned in a way where nothing interesting can happen: we can't really see the cool story of how the Foundation pulled this off without the UIU realising; and we can't really see a story of someone figuring out this has happened and like trying to stop it; and so there's not really a lot of room for you to do anything interesting with it? I also don't really think that just setting up what happened here is interesting enough because it doesn't really have…a sense of there being consequences cos this happened? Like, a short article where you piece together this happened could almost work as long as there's a bit where it makes you realise why what happened is shocking and I'm not sure this has that?

+ Open for critique

This idea feels like you started with the house memory concept then forced a narrative around it that doesn't really make sense with it. These are pulling in different directions. While this is nitpicky, it feels very odd that this child, an amateur thaumaturge, would be able to curse a house with shapeshifters, a lure ability, and manage to corrupt themselves. While the last point makes sense, it feels like they succeeded if their mission was to curse a house.

What exactly are the d-class mission going to reveal in this article? As of right now, it feels tacked on as a way of adding length. Is the stinger going to be found here? I suppose yes but your narrative leads me to believe that everything about this family will be revealed before this happens. Also, what would the stinger be?

As of right now, I do not feel confident enough to greenlight this idea.

While this has somewhat interesting ideas in how it handles 4000 lore and Santa Claus, I feel it fails to explore them in sufficient depth for it to be a satisfying article. -1


Forum category: Per Page Discussions / Per page discussions
Forum thread: SCP-5925

+1

At first when I got that it was the Trolley Problem I thought it would be just a cheap ethical experiment and probably downvote. But in the end it is a very interesting logical exercise using the Problem just as a device. Indeed, for me it highlights just how obtuse is the Trolley Problem and the two extreme takes on ethics it clashes.

For me the convoluted procedure justifies itself on the basis of reliability. Six can't say what happens if the dog is killed or if they kills themself. There is a need to keep things going if Six dies first. Also Six cannot guarantee their own follow-up of procedure if put under constant direct moral stress.

Deontology focus on action doesn't mean that it affords complete inaction, either. The Trolley problem puts 1 life against 5 because even for a deontologist it would be immoral to kill through inaction if the saving action had no moral consequence. More importantly, what's at stake isn't arguing how deontology works, but how the anomaly will interpret it, and then a less complex procedure would carry the risk of a breach.

item.title: Seeking greenlight for SCP
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre: Horror

Elevator Pitch: An archive of written material that has been lost to the rest of the world. Deleted files, burned documents, things like that. Some of this information would be very dangerous if it got out. The archive and its contents are usually imperceptible, but Foundation mnestics allow it and the materials therin to be seen and remembered. However, mnestic drugs are not strong enough to perceive its guardian, who does not want intruders in its archive.

Central Narrative: Researchers initially appear to have only recently discovered the skip and are making plans to have it explored and studied further. Then someone realizes that they have documentation from prior testing and exploration that no one remembers ordering. They have apparently sent multiple D-Class and MTF agents into the skip, but none of them have come out. Also, no other documentation of the existence of said personnell exists outside of DEEPWELL archives. One agent emerges from the skip physically unharmed, but showing symptoms of psychological trauma. The agent can't remember what may have caused said trauma or why they are the only member of their task force on record. The Foundation can tell something is up and suspends testing. This is not the first time this sequence has repeated, perhaps end the article with the start of a new cycle of testing and forgetting.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: I really enjoy articles you have to think about to understand. I want to not actually state that there is a monster in the archive, rather I'd like to let readers figure that out on their own in a way that both makes them feel clever and accomplished and provides fridge horror type creep factor.

Additional Notes: I'm going to need help with the structure of the article if this ends up being something that interests people. I'll also need some help making the Foundation not look incompetent while preserving the mystery aspect. This needs to be something that seems reasonable for the Foundation to have misinterpreted.

item.title: [Seeking Greenlight] SCP Concept Critique
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout: Standard containment procedures and description, with background on its discovery. Interview and test logs showing how its anomalous effects were deduced, as well as further experimentation.

Elevator Pitch: A mattress/mattresses that induces vivid dreams in those who sleep in it. Upon waking up, their memories are retroactively altered to include, and frequently overridden with the contents of their dreams (e.g. a man who dreams of fishing may believe he had been a fisherman his whole life; a person who dreams of a deceased loved one believes they are still alive).

Central Narrative: A hospital gains Foundation attention after an outbreak of manic patients. Investigation leads to the discovery of the SCP. The affected patients are taken into Foundation custody to be examined so as to further understand the nature of the SCP.

The possibility of the SCP being used to treat treatment-resistant conditions is explored, leading to extensive testing. Humorous and dramatic attempts follow due to the SCP's unreliable nature.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: It's a memory-altering SCP that relies on the user's dreams to fabricate memories.

Additional Notes: I'm open to suggestions or developments to the concept and narrative.

item.title: Re: Ms. G. Lass
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there Angryman22. Let’s take a look at your concept.

It starts off promising, but I’m struggling to connect the various anomalous together. For example, what does a survivor of a glass factory explosion have to do with “a strong hatred for transparent objects”? Furthermore, why is it that when they’re “exposed to even a very small amount of oxygen, they will engulf in flames reaching a temperature of 4000K”?

You appear to be adding these anomalous properties without consideration for purpose or reason. At best, this sounds like a possible body horror scip if you manage to delve deeper into the psychology of the humanoid. Tell us more about who Georgine Lass was/is. Why is she behaving the way she is after the explosion? At worst, however, this scip sounds like your typical Peter Parker-gets-bitten-by-a-radioactive-spider-and-becomes-a-superhero sort of story. Even then, you need to flesh out the character’s motivations and goals and tell us why she’s behaving as such.

If you decide to revise the concept / respond below, do drop me another PM and I’ll take another look. For now, all the best!

item.title: Re: "When We Didn't Dream" - An SCP Tale Seeking Greenlight
item.content:encoded:
Summoned via PM:

Hi there gravyismad. So I'm close to a greenlight for this, mainly because you've chosen to base your Tale on an existing SCP and the way you've outlined your story clearly shows you've given it some thought.

My only concern right now is the ending. Could you elaborate a bit more on how you want the story to end? At the moment, it sounds bleak: he comes to the realisation that there's no hope? And then what? Ideally, there should be some kind of bittersweetness to an ending: he gains something, but at the cost of something else.

Summoned via Pm
Interesting SCP you've got there
It would be a shame if someone…
Critiqued it…

+ show block
– hide block

So while this idea has some potential, there are a LOT of things you need to fix before I (and many other concept reviewers) will consider giving you a greenlight.

  • Elevator pitch: Don't tell me your idea isn't special. You're trying to sell me on the idea, so you need to be confident about it. Writing "um this book isn't special" is an immediate turn off. Try and find something unique. It doesn't have to be revolutionary or groundbreaking: just unique and intriguing enough to get someone to read through it.
  • Central Narrative: I'm sorry, but I barely understand the story you're going for. Where did the entity come from? Why did the serpent's hand ally with the Foundation? What brought SCP-1000 into the situation? You need to make your idea more concise. It's barely half baked right now: mising al the details that a successful article has. You honestly need to work on your idea before moving forward.
  • Hook: You need more than just a pair of O5s to get your story to appear interesting. Tel me why I should read your article rather than another article. Also, where did Merlin come from?
  • Additional Notes: This idea needs to go back in the oven IT's lacking the crucial components and skill necessary for creating a coherent and compelling piece. This idea is salvageable, but you need to really work on your writing skills. Apologies if anything here sounded rude, as that was not my intent.

item.title: "The Homeless Man" - SCP Idea - GL
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Genre (Optional): Horror

Elevator Pitch:

A humanoid figure looking like a starving man.
Any human who goes near it that laughs gets attacked, bitten/ripped, and peeled by the SCP.
He's locked in a simple windowless room.

Central Narrative:

Starts off in urban Florida 2019, where the SCP was presumed to be a homeless man living on the street.
It was there for 2 years, not doing anything until it was caught trying to peel (with teeth) a local teen's skin off.
Video footage was captured (eventually uploaded online), and the SCP quickly-crawled away with the body.

+ show block
– hide block

Foundation field agents were warned and investigated after widespread local fear of SCP-XXXX online.
MTF Search-Teams found SCP-XXXX by an urban lake.
SCP's didn't eat, breathe, talk or scream, and walked on all fours similar to a spider.
It was captured by MTF. (Audio Attached)

Foundation put coverup stories, making a fake background, court charges, and sentencing.
Foundation took a list of items where SCP was recorded: Printed photos of people of ranging ages and an old coat SCP wore made of skin parts of different animals.

Research on the photos (attached) revealed the people were that of now-dead people.
People were that of children, adults, prison inmates, and one of the leading researchers of the Foundation.
Connections between lists of people could not be found by staff, but details of who they are, are given.
Hidden letters on the photos revealed words "fam", "peel", "ric", "sorrow", "controlling", "it's gone", and "give it back".
A note was found in the coat that stated "Life is given to those with lemons, a bad one is given to those with oranges".

D-class was used to experiment on the SCP, audio recordings, and experiment chart was attached.
SCP-XXXX didn't react or attack until the third experiment, where the D-Class chuckled nervously.
More experiments occurred until Foundation found out SCP-XXXX only reacts to D-class laughing at certain distances.

SCP-XXXX was watched over after every kill, in which he was seen to make shapes with the pieces of skin.
Foundation gave SCP-XXXX crayons and paper, but it only used skin to make shapes.
Recreated drawings were made (and attached), with the most identifiable ones as an orange, a house, a frowning face, and a knife.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Creepiness is from lack of info on the lore.

item.title: Re: What is the **out** of universe reason for discontinuing MTF Omega 7 Pandoras Box?
item.content:encoded:
From what I've read, it was a good idea that was taken out of hand. We're trying to give it another shot with Alpha-9, but the key is, we need to stop thinking X-Men and more Suicide Squad. When I first got here and found out about these MTFs, my thinking was that it is very hard to contain all these things and if some are useful, use them, and if some are people who may be cooperative, make them earn their keep. The idea should be SCPs are being put to work because it's expensive to house and feed them so the least they can do is help when we need them, assuming they will help at all. But it turns into a Mary-Sue fest because people want to make superheroes from anomalies instead of considering SCPs as horrors first and a last resort to solve other problems when nothing else works. Omega-7 went off the rails and the authors put the rabid beast down, and if we are going to give it a second shot, make sure the writers know the idea is anomalies that got caught and are out on work release.

item.title: Re: What is the first scp?
item.content:encoded:
My theory: The first SCP is either 557 or 2932, or perhaps, more precisely, what's contained in them. SCP 2932 is a Thaumiel made by the Children of the Night, meaning it predates humanity and contained what were basically the first SCPs from prehistoric times. 557 is the Ancient Containment site, and my theory is that 557-1(the prisoner) is actually 682, but that was secondary, its primary purpose was to contain 2317 Prime, with 2317 itself actually being only the back door. I mean, did anyone think 2317-K was coming out that little door? No, he was sealed in under 557, the stone in the floor is the key to the seal and thats where he's coming out when the last chain breaks. Why 2317 was made, I don't know, but my guess it was either cultists who couldn't find the main entrance or Jailors who wanted to check and make sure SCP-001 hadn't already escaped without breaking the seal.
